claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Gascoigne et al., 2011; Przewloka et al., 2011; Hori et al., 2013.

claims.claim: In C. elegans CENP-C localizes to chromatin only during mitosis, but not interphase, when it is in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: Although CENP-C remains with centromeric DNA throughout the cell cycle in other organisms, in C. elegans CENP-C localizes to chromatin only during mitosis, but not interphase, when it is in the cytoplasm (Moore and Roth, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Moore and Roth, 2001.

claims.claim: CENP-C is enriched at cenH3 sites.
claims.source: We found that CENP-C is enriched at cenH3 sites (Figure 4A,C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 4A and 4C.

claims.claim: 460 of the 2060 insoluble chromatin peaks coincided with cenH3 peaks.
claims.source: Despite the presence of non-centromeric enrichment in the insoluble chromatin fraction and the lower dynamic range of the CENP-C ChIP data, we called peaks in these two data sets and compared them to the cenH3 peak calls. 460 of the 2060 insoluble chromatin peaks and 163 of the 347 insoluble chromatin peaks coincided with cenH3 peaks.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on peak calling analysis.

claims.claim: 163 of the 347 CENP-C peaks coincided with cenH3 peaks.
claims.source: Despite the presence of non-centromeric enrichment in the insoluble chromatin fraction and the lower dynamic range of the CENP-C ChIP data, we called peaks in these two data sets and compared them to the cenH3 peak calls. 460 of the 2060 insoluble chromatin peaks and 163 of the 347 insoluble chromatin peaks coincided with cenH3 peaks.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on peak calling analysis.

claims.claim: Only 174 insoluble chromatin peaks and 26 CENP-C peaks fell within the domains, in both cases fewer sites than expected by chance.
claims.source: In contrast, only 174 insoluble chromatin peaks and 26 CENP-C peaks fell within the domains, in both cases fewer sites than expected by chance (p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on peak calling analysis.

claims.claim: There is an 800-fold enrichment of insoluble chromatin peaks at cenH3 peaks compared to cenH3 domains.
claims.source: Normalized to the genome coverage of domains and peaks, this amounts to an 800-fold enrichment of insoluble chromatin peaks and an almost 2000-fold enrichment of CENP-C peaks at cenH3 peaks compared to cenH3 domains (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and 2D.

claims.claim: There is an almost 2000-fold enrichment of CENP-C peaks at cenH3 peaks compared to cenH3 domains.
claims.source: Normalized to the genome coverage of domains and peaks, this amounts to an 800-fold enrichment of insoluble chromatin peaks and an almost 2000-fold enrichment of CENP-C peaks at cenH3 peaks compared to cenH3 domains (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and 2D.

claims.claim: The cenH3 peaks identified in this study act as the preferred sites of kinetochore formation.
claims.source: These results indicate that the cenH3 peaks identified in this study act as the preferred sites of kinetochore formation.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the co-localization of cenH3, CENP-C, and insoluble chromatin peaks.

claims.claim: The number of cenH3 sites lies in the same order of magnitude as the number of microtubules observed during mitosis.
claims.source: Moreover, the number of sites lies in the same order of magnitude as the number of microtubules observed during mitosis, thus providing a mechanistically reasonable alternative to the conundrum of how domains that cover half of the genome can organize a relatively small number of microtubule attachment sites.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the number of cenH3 sites identified and comparison to the known number of microtubules.

claims.claim: Centromeric nucleosomes in other organisms protect only 80–120 bp of wrapped DNA, compared to 147 bp for canonical nucleosomes.
claims.source: Centromeric nucleosomes in other organisms protect only 80–120 bp of wrapped DNA, compared to 147 bp for canonical nucleosomes (Dalal et al., 2007; Krassovsky et al., 2012; Hasson et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013), probably due to the reduced wrapping of DNA around them (Henikoff and Furuyama, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Dalal et al., 2007; Krassovsky et al., 2012; Hasson et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013; Henikoff and Furuyama, 2012.

claims.claim: Two well-positioned nucleosomes flank the cenH3 peaks.
claims.source: In the input sample, we found that two well-positioned nucleosomes flank the cenH3 peaks (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The native input sample revealed the presence of sub-nucleosome-size fragments over the center of the cenH3 sites.
claims.source: The native input sample also revealed the presence of sub-nucleosome-size fragments over the center of the cenH3 sites, while few of these fragments were found in the flanking regions (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In the cenH3 ChIP sample, only relatively few nucleosome-size fragments were recovered, while the majority of the signal came from fragments <140 bp.
claims.source: In the cenH3 ChIP sample, only relatively few nucleosome-size fragments were recovered, while the majority of the signal came from fragments <140 bp (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The insoluble chromatin showed a similar pattern to the cenH3 ChIP sample, indicating that the particles bound to DNA at cenH3 sites are similar in the insoluble and in the soluble chromatin fractions.
claims.source: The insoluble chromatin showed a similar pattern, indicating that the particles bound to DNA at cenH3 sites are similar in the insoluble and in the soluble chromatin fractions (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Centromeric sites consist of two well-positioned nucleosomes flanking a single cenH3 nucleosome that wraps less DNA than is wrapped by a canonical nucleosome.
claims.source: This analysis showed that centromeric sites consist of two well-positioned nucleosomes flanking a single cenH3 nucleosome that wraps less DNA than is wrapped by a canonical nucleosome.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on fragment size analysis data.

claims.claim: In the input sample after 2 min of MNase digestion, the fragments that cross the dyad of the flanking nucleosomes show a distribution that peaks at 166 bp, consistent with canonical nucleosomes.
claims.source: In the input sample after 2 min of MNase digestion, the fragments that cross the dyad of the flanking nucleosomes show a distribution that peaks at 166 bp, consistent with canonical nucleosomes (Figure 5E, black line).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The fragments that cross the center of the cenH3 nucleosomes in the cenH3 ChIP sample after 2 min of MNase digestion indicate that the nucleosomes that occupy these sites protect only about 60–120 bp.
claims.source: The fragments that cross the center of the cenH3 nucleosomes in the cenH3 ChIP sample after 2 min of MNase digestion show a strikingly different distribution that is left-shifted and indicate that the nucleosomes that occupy these sites protect only about 60–120 bp (Figure 5E, blue line).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: After 10 min of MNase digestion, the peak of the distribution of MNase fragments that cross the center of the cenH3 sites in the insoluble fractions lies at 66 bp.
claims.source: After 10 min of MNase digestion, the peak of the distribution of MNase fragments that cross the center of the cenH3 sites in the insoluble fractions lies at 66 bp (Figure 5F, magenta line), indicating that the minimal protected size of these particles lies in the 60–100 bp range.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The inferred fragment size protected by the centromeric nucleosome is 60–100 bp.
claims.source: Moreover, the width at half-height of the average 10 min-digested insoluble chromatin peak that aligns with the cenH3 peaks is 82 bp (Figure 5—figure supplement 3). The inferred fragment size protected by the centromeric nucleosome is thus 60–100 bp.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on fragment size analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: CenH3 nucleosomes at centromeric sites in C. elegans wrap less DNA than that wrapped by canonical nucleosomes.
claims.source: These results confirm the findings in other organisms that cenH3 nucleosomes at centromeric sites in C. elegans wrap less DNA than that wrapped by canonical nucleosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on fragment size analysis data and comparison to other organisms.

claims.claim: The majority of cenH3 nucleosomes in domains protect about 135–155 bp of DNA.
claims.source: Fragment size analysis revealed that the majority of cenH3 nucleosomes in these regions of the genome protect about 135–155 bp of DNA, and that this size distribution is similar in regions between domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: CenH3 can incorporate into canonical-type nucleosomes away from centromeres, in some cases as cenH3-H3.3 heterotypic nucleosomes.
claims.source: This level of protection is consistent with the findings in other organisms that cenH3 can incorporate into canonical-type nucleosomes away from centromeres, in some cases as cenH3-H3.3 heterotypic nucleosomes (Camahort et al., 2009; Krassovsky et al., 2012; Lacoste et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Camahort et al., 2009; Krassovsky et al., 2012; Lacoste et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The cenH3 domains may be distributed independently of the centromere.
claims.source: This further suggests that the cenH3 domains may be distributed independently of the centromere.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the fragment size analysis of cenH3 nucleosomes in domains.

claims.claim: Each centromeric site consists of a single cenH3-containing nucleosome that is flanked by two well-positioned canonical nucleosomes.
claims.source: Taken together, fragment size analysis thus revealed that each centromeric site consists of a single cenH3-containing nucleosome that is flanked by two well-positioned canonical nucleosomes (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on fragment size analysis data, illustrated in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The chromatin landscape of C. elegans centromeric sites is reminiscent of the budding yeast centromere.
claims.source: This chromatin landscape is reminiscent of the budding yeast centromere, where a single cenH3 nucleosome assembles on a genetically defined sequence (Furuyama and Biggins, 2007; Henikoff and Henikoff, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to established knowledge about budding yeast centromeres, supported by citations to Furuyama and Biggins, 2007 and Henikoff and Henikoff, 2012.

claims.claim: In budding yeast, the centromeric sequence is flanked by binding sites for centromere-specific protein complexes (Cbf1 and Cbf3) that in turn position two flanking canonical nucleosomes.
claims.source: This sequence is flanked by binding sites for centromere-specific protein complexes (Cbf1 and Cbf3) that in turn position two flanking canonical nucleosomes (Figure 5H) (Densmore et al., 1991; Krassovsky et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about budding yeast centromeres, supported by citations to Densmore et al., 1991 and Krassovsky et al., 2012, illustrated in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The stable binding of Cbf1 and Cbf3 prevent the centromeric DNA from being occupied by canonical nucleosomes in budding yeast.
claims.source: The stable binding of Cbf1 and Cbf3 prevent the centromeric DNA from being occupied by canonical nucleosomes (Kent et al., 2011; Krassovsky et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about budding yeast centromeres, supported by citations to Kent et al., 2011 and Krassovsky et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In C. elegans, the flanking nucleosomes are positioned closer together than in yeast, presumably because there are no sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins between the centromeric and the flanking nucleosomes.
claims.source: In C. elegans, the flanking nucleosomes are positioned closer together than in yeast, presumably because there are no sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins between the centromeric and the flanking nucleosomes.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of the chromatin landscape in C. elegans to that in budding yeast.

claims.claim: The dispersed centromeric sites in C. elegans holocentromeres consist of a cenH3 nucleosome that is associated with 60–100 bp of DNA flanked by two well-positioned nucleosomes, a chromatin pattern with striking similarities to budding yeast point centromeres.
claims.source: Thus, the dispersed centromeric sites in C. elegans holocentromeres consist of a cenH3 nucleosome that is associated with 60–100 bp of DNA flanked by two well-positioned nucleosomes, a chromatin pattern with striking similarities to budding yeast point centromeres.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fragment size analysis and comparison to budding yeast.

claims.claim: Budding yeast point centromeres assemble on a genetically defined sequence.
claims.source: Budding yeast point centromeres assemble on a genetically defined sequence (Clarke and Carbon, 1980).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Clarke and Carbon, 1980.

claims.claim: A 15-nt GA-repeat-rich motif was common to 297 of the 80-bp cores of the centromeric sites.
claims.source: We found a 15-nt GA-repeat-rich motif that was common to 297 of the 80-bp cores of the centromeric sites (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: A weaker, but similar GA-rich motif was common to all 707 centromeric sites.
claims.source: A weaker, but similar GA-rich motif was common to all 707 centromeric sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The 15-nt motif also matched more than 60,000 sites in the genome that are not associated with high cenH3 signal and so is not sufficient to determine cenH3 occupancy.
claims.source: The 15-nt motif also matched more than 60,000 sites in the genome that are not associated with high cenH3 signal and so is not sufficient to determine cenH3 occupancy.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on motif analysis.

claims.claim: GAGA-rich sequences are well-characterized targets for the GAGA factor (GAF/Trl) in D. melanogaster.
claims.source: GAGA-rich sequences are well-characterized targets for the GAGA factor (GAF/Trl) in D. melanogaster (van Steensel et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to van Steensel et al., 2003.

claims.claim: A GAF/Trl homologue could not be identified in the C. elegans genome.
claims.source: However, we could not identify a GAF/Trl homologue in the C. elegans genome.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on genome analysis.

claims.claim: The motif identified at centromeric sites is almost identical to the motif associated with C. elegans high occupancy target (HOT) sites.
claims.source: Instead, the motif we identified is almost identical to the motif associated with C. elegans high occupancy target (HOT) sites (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by motif comparison shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: HOT sites were uncovered by the modENCODE consortium through binding-site analysis of 22 transcription factors and operationally defined as sites that are bound by ≥15 transcription factors.
claims.source: These sites were uncovered by the modENCODE consortium through binding-site analysis of 22 transcription factors and operationally defined as sites that are bound by ≥15 transcription factors (Gerstein et al., 2010; Niu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Gerstein et al., 2010 and Niu et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The sequences at HOT sites do not contain DNA motifs of known C. elegans transcription factors and are therefore expected to bind transcription factors with low affinity.
claims.source: The sequences at these sites do not contain DNA motifs of known C. elegans transcription factors and are therefore expected to bind transcription factors with low affinity.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about HOT sites.

claims.claim: 117 out of 248 HOT sites coincided with cenH3 sites.
claims.source: We found that 117 out of 248 HOT sites coincided with cenH3 sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; hypergeometric p=8.6 × 10−161).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The actual overlap of cenH3 sites and transcription factor hotspots is likely to be much larger than 117 out of 248, given that only 22 transcription factors have been used for the definition of HOT sites, but that there are 934 predicted transcription factors encoded in the C. elegans genome.
claims.source: Although this degree of overlap is striking, the actual overlap of cenH3 sites and transcription factor hotspots is likely to be much larger, given the fact that that only 22 transcription factors have been used for the definition of HOT sites, but that there are 934 predicted transcription factors encoded in the C. elegans genome (Reece-Hoyes et al., 2005; Gerstein et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the overlap analysis and known number of transcription factors in C. elegans, supported by citations to Reece-Hoyes et al., 2005 and Gerstein et al., 2010.

claims.claim: HOT sites show a high signal for cenH3 ChIP, insoluble chromatin, and CENP-C ChIP.
claims.source: We also found that HOT sites show a high signal for cenH3 ChIP, insoluble chromatin, CENP-C ChIP (Figure 6B) and well-positioned flanking nucleosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The cenH3 ChIP signal at HOT sites is reduced in KNL-2-depleted animals.
claims.source: Moreover, the cenH3 ChIP signal is reduced in KNL-2-depleted animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claims.claim: HOT sites and centromeric sites share a similar chromatin landscape and are targeted by both cenH3 nucleosomes and transcription factors.
claims.source: These data suggest that HOT sites and centromeric sites share a similar chromatin landscape and are targeted by both cenH3 nucleosomes and transcription factors.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the overlap and chromatin landscape analysis of HOT sites and centromeric sites.

claims.claim: CenH3 protein is below detection levels in adult muscle cells.
claims.source: To probe the chromatin landscape in cenH3-depleted cells, we analyzed our previously published data for affinity-purified adult muscle cells, where cenH3 protein is below detection levels (Figure 7A), and cenH3 mRNA is significantly depleted (Bayesian t-test; q = 0.0036) (Steiner et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors, supported by data shown in Figure 7A and citation to Steiner et al., 2012.

claims.claim: CenH3 mRNA is significantly depleted in adult muscle cells.
claims.source: To probe the chromatin landscape in cenH3-depleted cells, we analyzed our previously published data for affinity-purified adult muscle cells, where cenH3 protein is below detection levels (Figure 7A), and cenH3 mRNA is significantly depleted (Bayesian t-test; q = 0.0036) (Steiner et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors, supported by citation to Steiner et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In total adult samples, which contain nuclei from dividing germline and embryonic cells, there was a depletion of signal at centromeric sites and well-positioned nucleosomes flanking the sites.
claims.source: In total adult samples, which contain nuclei from dividing germline and embryonic cells, we found a depletion of signal at centromeric sites and well-positioned nucleosomes flanking the sites, reminiscent of the chromatin landscape in embryos (Figure 7B, black line).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: In muscle nuclei, the flanking nucleosomes were present.
claims.source: In muscle nuclei, the flanking nucleosomes were also present (Figure 7B, red line), and protected a very similar size range of fragments as in the total nuclei sample (Figure 7C, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: The centromeric sites in the muscle nuclei sample were occupied by MNase-stable particles.
claims.source: However, the centromeric sites in the muscle nuclei sample were occupied by MNase-stable particles (Figure 7B, red line) that protect sub-nucleosome-size fragments (Figure 7C, right panel) and likely represent non-nucleosomal DNA-binding proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: HLH-1 is the C. elegans myoD homologue and is required for proper myogenesis.
claims.source: HLH-1 is the C. elegans myoD homologue and is required for proper myogenesis (Krause, 1995).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Krause, 1995.

claims.claim: HLH-1 is exclusively expressed in the same cells that have been used for the muscle chromatin profiling.
claims.source: It is exclusively expressed in the same cells that have been used for the muscle chromatin profiling (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: HLH-1 is enriched at the majority of centromeric sites.
claims.source: We found that HLH-1 is enriched at the majority of centromeric sites (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: All tested transcription factors profiled in larval instar 2 or later stages are enriched at centromeric sites.
claims.source: We found that all tested transcription factors profiled in larval instar 2 or later stages, when few somatic cells are still dividing, are enriched at centromeric sites (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: If cenH3 is depleted, centromeric sites are not occupied by canonical nucleosomes, but are bound by sub-nucleosome-size particles at least some of which are known transcription factors.
claims.source: These results show that if cenH3 is depleted, centromeric sites are not occupied by canonical nucleosomes, but are bound by sub-nucleosome-size particles at least some of which are known transcription factors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of muscle nuclei and transcription factor ChIP data.

claims.claim: Some HOT sites have post-mitotic functions as enhancers.
claims.source: As centromere function is needed only in dividing cells, this possibility is consistent with the observation that some HOT sites have post-mitotic functions as enhancers (Kvon et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Kvon et al., 2012 and Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Holocentricity is a common mode of chromosome organization, having evolved from monocentricity at least 13 times, including organisms as diverse as nematodes, moths, and sedges.
claims.source: Holocentricity is a common mode of chromosome organization, having evolved from monocentricity at least 13 times, including organisms as diverse as nematodes, moths, and sedges (Melters et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Melters et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The polycentromere model is correct for C. elegans.
claims.source: We use high resolution mapping of centromeric nucleosomes to demonstrate that the polycentromere model is correct for C. elegans, and that C. elegans holocentromeres consist of about 100 centromeric sites on each chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the high-resolution mapping data presented in the study.

claims.claim: C. elegans holocentromeres consist of about 100 centromeric sites on each chromosome.
claims.source: We use high resolution mapping of centromeric nucleosomes to demonstrate that the polycentromere model is correct for C. elegans, and that C. elegans holocentromeres consist of about 100 centromeric sites on each chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on peak calling analysis.

claims.claim: The number of discrete centromeric sites is in excess over the observed number of microtubule attachments.
claims.source: The number of discrete centromeric sites is in excess over the observed number of microtubule attachments, which has been estimated to be ∼100 for all six chromosomes by electron tomography (O'Toole et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's findings to established knowledge, supported by citation to O'Toole et al., 2003.

claims.claim: It is possible that only about 15% of the centromeric sites identified in this study are attached in each mitotic cell.
claims.source: It is possible that only about 15% of the centromeric sites identified in this study are attached in each mitotic cell, which seems reasonable given that we analyzed a diverse cell population.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the number of centromeric sites and the number of microtubule attachments.

claims.claim: The availability of multiple centromeric sites might reflect redundancy to assure faithful segregation in every cell cycle.
claims.source: The availability of multiple centromeric sites might reflect redundancy to assure faithful segregation in every cell cycle, although it is also possible that some sites are rendered inaccessible for cenH3 nucleosomes in some cell lineages due to changes in expression profiles during development.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of multiple centromeric sites.

claims.claim: Some centromeric sites might be rendered inaccessible for cenH3 nucleosomes in some cell lineages due to changes in expression profiles during development.
claims.source: The availability of multiple centromeric sites might reflect redundancy to assure faithful segregation in every cell cycle, although it is also possible that some sites are rendered inaccessible for cenH3 nucleosomes in some cell lineages due to changes in expression profiles during development.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the regulation of centromeric sites during development.

claims.claim: A large fraction of cenH3 is incorporated into broad domains that cover half of the genome.
claims.source: Polycentromere and diffuse centromere mechanisms might not be mutually exclusive, insofar as a large fraction of cenH3 is incorporated into broad domains that cover half of the genome.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous studies.

claims.claim: The domains are in part shaped by transcription in the germline and are present in the early embryo.
claims.source: The domains are in part shaped by transcription in the germline and are present in the early embryo, however, there is no significant RNA Pol II-dependent transcription during the first two rounds of embryonic cell division.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous studies.

claims.claim: H3.3 is retained both in mature sperm and oocytes, suggesting that it transmits epigenetic information through both the maternal and the paternal germline.
claims.source: Specifically, H3.3 is retained both in mature sperm and oocytes, suggesting that it transmits epigenetic information through both the maternal and the paternal germline.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about H3.3.

claims.claim: The maintenance of H3.3 in sperm might explain how the domain pattern is established on paternal chromatin upon fertilization, even though cenH3 is not maintained in mature sperm.
claims.source: The maintenance of H3.3 in sperm might explain how the domain pattern is established on paternal chromatin upon fertilization, even though cenH3 is not maintained in mature sperm (Gassmann et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the properties of H3.3 and cenH3, supported by citation to Gassmann et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The domains probably do not have a direct centromere function, although they might serve as cenH3 'reservoirs'.
claims.source: However, because these domains do not align with the kinetochore, they probably do not have a direct centromere function, although they might serve as cenH3 'reservoirs', in parallel with the suggestion that Drosophila transcription factor hotspots might serve as transcription factor reservoirs (Moorman et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the lack of alignment between domains and kinetochores, with comparison to Drosophila transcription factor hotspots, supported by citation to Moorman et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Individual centromeric sites resemble budding yeast point centromeres: a single cenH3 nucleosome flanked by two well-positioned nucleosomes.
claims.source: We have found that individual centromeric sites resemble budding yeast point centromeres: a single cenH3 nucleosome flanked by two well-positioned nucleosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chromatin landscape analysis.

claims.claim: Satellite repeats help position centromeric nucleosomes at regional centromeres in many species.
claims.source: Point centromeres are genetically defined in budding yeast, and satellite repeats help position centromeric nucleosomes at regional centromeres in many species.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of centromere biology.

claims.claim: Neo-centromeres can form on sequences that are not normally linked to centromeres.
claims.source: However, neo-centromeres can form on sequences that are not normally linked to centromeres (Marshall et al., 2008; Shang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Marshall et al., 2008 and Shang et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Centromeric nucleosomes are inherited in a sequence-independent way.
claims.source: These observations suggest that centromeric nucleosomes are inherited in a sequence-independent way, so that it might seem surprising that a distinct sequence motif is associated with C. elegans centromeric sites.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of neo-centromeres.

claims.claim: The DNA at centromeric sites might disfavor the formation of canonical nucleosomes, allowing centromeric nucleosomes to form in these 'gaps' in the chromatin landscape.
claims.source: However, given that the motif is short and its abundance in the genome by far exceeds the number of centromeric sites, there is no evidence that it is a direct target for cenH3-nucleosome loading. Rather, the DNA at these sites might disfavor the formation of canonical nucleosomes, allowing centromeric nucleosomes to form in these 'gaps' in the chromatin landscape.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the properties of the motif and the chromatin landscape.

claims.claim: A similar model for worm holocentromeres had been proposed by Gu and Fire based on finding ∼120-bp 'holes' in the nucleosome landscape that could fit small nucleosomes the size of those previously shown for Drosophila cenH3.
claims.source: A similar model for worm holocentromeres had been proposed by Gu and Fire (Gu and Fire, 2010) based on finding ∼120-bp 'holes' in the nucleosome landscape that could fit small nucleosomes the size of those previously shown for Drosophila cenH3 (Dalal et al., 2007).

results.result: C. elegans holocentromeres are organized as dispersed point centromeres consisting of approximately 100 discrete sites per chromosome (707 total), each containing a single cenH3 nucleosome flanked by two well-positioned canonical nucleosomes. The sites are separated by distances ranging from 290 bp to 1.9 Mb (median 83 kb).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C36, C37, C85, C90, C117, and C118 are directly supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 1), fragment size analysis (Figure 5), and peak calling showing 707 cenH3 peaks. The structural characterization showing single cenH3 nucleosomes flanked by canonical nucleosomes is supported by fragment size distributions (C77-C80, Figure 5E-F). This represents the core finding of the manuscript with converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: Centromeric sites co-localize with kinetochore components, with CENP-C showing enrichment at cenH3 sites and 163 of 347 CENP-C peaks coinciding with cenH3 peaks, representing an almost 2000-fold enrichment at cenH3 peaks compared to cenH3 domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C63, C64, C65, C67, C68, and C69 are supported by CENP-C ChIP data (Figure 4A, 4C) and insoluble chromatin analysis (Figure 4A, 4B) showing co-localization with cenH3 peaks. The enrichment calculations (C67, C68) are based on peak calling and normalization to genome coverage (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D). The data demonstrate functional kinetochore assembly at these sites.

results.result: Centromeric site occupancy depends on the cenH3 loading machinery, as KNL-2 depletion by RNAi causes embryonic lethality (99±1% penetrance), chromosome segregation defects, and much reduced cenH3 occupancy at centromeric sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C47, C48, C49, C50, C52, and C57 are supported by KNL-2 RNAi experiments showing reduced cenH3 ChIP signal at centromeric sites (Figure 3) and reduced insoluble chromatin signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B). The embryonic lethality phenotype and chromosome segregation defects provide functional validation. The control showing unchanged input chromatin (C51) strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: CenH3 peaks are hypersensitive to MNase digestion compared to flanking nucleosomes and +1 nucleosomes, disappearing with progressive MNase digestion even under conditions where nucleosome arrays remain intact.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, C45, and C46 are supported by MNase time-course experiments (Figure 2A-D) showing differential sensitivity of cenH3 nucleosomes versus flanking nucleosomes. The quantification in Figure 2D demonstrates that cenH3 nucleosomes are more sensitive than both flanking and +1 nucleosomes. This is consistent with properties of centromeric nucleosomes in other organisms (C42).

results.result: Centromeric sites consist of two well-positioned nucleosomes flanking a single cenH3 nucleosome that protects 60-100 bp of DNA, less than the 147 bp protected by canonical nucleosomes. Fragment size analysis shows peaks at 166 bp for flanking nucleosomes and 60-120 bp for cenH3 nucleosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C81 are supported by comprehensive fragment size analysis (Figure 5A-F) showing distinct size distributions for cenH3 nucleosomes versus flanking nucleosomes. The 60-100 bp protection estimate is based on multiple lines of evidence including ChIP fragment sizes (C78), insoluble chromatin fragments (C79), and half-height width measurements (C80, Figure 5—figure supplement 3). This confirms findings in other organisms (C71, C81).

results.result: Centromeric sites coincide with high occupancy target (HOT) sites, with 117 of 248 HOT sites overlapping with cenH3 sites (hypergeometric p=8.6×10⁻¹⁶¹). A 15-nt GA-repeat-rich motif is common to centromeric sites and is almost identical to the HOT site motif.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C92, C93, C94, C97, C100, C101, C102, and C104 are supported by motif analysis (Figure 6A) and overlap analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). The statistical significance of the overlap is strong (p=8.6×10⁻¹⁶¹). HOT sites show high signal for cenH3 ChIP, insoluble chromatin, and CENP-C ChIP (Figure 6B, C102). The interpretation that actual overlap may be larger (C101) is reasonable given limited transcription factor profiling.

results.result: When cenH3 is lost in adult muscle cells, centromeric sites become occupied by transcription factors including HLH-1, with sites occupied by MNase-stable sub-nucleosome-size particles rather than canonical nucleosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C103, C105, C106, C107, C108, C109, C112, C113, and C114 are supported by analysis of adult muscle cells where cenH3 protein is below detection (Figure 7A) and cenH3 mRNA is significantly depleted (q=0.0036, C106). MNase-seq shows centromeric sites occupied by sub-nucleosome particles (Figure 7B-C), and HLH-1 ChIP shows enrichment at centromeric sites (Figure 7D). Multiple transcription factors show enrichment (Figure 7E, C113).

results.result: The point centromere is the basic unit of holocentric organization, supporting the classical polycentric model. Individual centromeric sites resemble budding yeast point centromeres with striking similarities in chromatin landscape.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C86, and C128 represent the main conclusion of the study, supported by the structural characterization showing single cenH3 nucleosomes flanked by canonical nucleosomes (Figure 5G-H). The comparison to budding yeast is appropriate given the similar chromatin architecture (C87, C88), though C. elegans sites lack sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins between nucleosomes (C89). This conclusion integrates multiple lines of evidence from the study.

results.result: CenH3 is enriched toward chromosome arms and positively correlates with H3K9me3 (r=0.44, p<2.2×10⁻¹⁶) and negatively correlates with H3.3 (r=-0.65, p<2.2×10⁻¹⁶), suggesting nucleosome turnover excludes cenH3 deposition and shapes the domain-like distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C23, C27, and C34 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) with statistically significant correlations. The interpretation that nucleosome turnover shapes cenH3 distribution (C34) is reasonable given the correlations with H3K9me3 (low turnover marker) and H3.3 (turnover marker). This is consistent with established knowledge about these histone marks (C24, C26, C33).

results.result: CenH3 occupies broad 10-12 kb domains covering about half the genome, with the current N-ChIP data showing similar domain patterns to previous X-ChIP data (r=0.67, p<2.2×10⁻¹⁶). However, 607 of 707 cenH3 peaks reside outside these previously described domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C30, C31, C40, C41, and C123 are supported by comparison of N-ChIP-seq to previous X-ChIP-chip data (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B). The high correlation (r=0.67) validates the domain pattern despite methodological differences. The finding that most peaks lie outside domains (C40) is a key observation distinguishing peaks from domains. This reconciles the diffuse and polycentric models.

results.result: Insoluble chromatin peaks correspond to cenH3 peaks and are more resistant to MNase than cenH3 nucleosomes in the soluble fraction, persisting after 10 min MNase digestion, suggesting proteins rendering chromatin insoluble protect it from nuclease digestion.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C58, and C59 are supported by analysis of insoluble chromatin showing peaks at cenH3 sites (Figure 4A-B) with greater MNase resistance than soluble cenH3 nucleosomes. The interpretation that kinetochore proteins provide protection (C59) is reasonable given the co-localization with CENP-C and the precedent from budding yeast (C54, C55). The reduction in knl-2(RNAi) (C57) supports this interpretation.

results.result: The number of cenH3 sites (~700) is in the same order of magnitude as the number of microtubules observed during mitosis (~100 for all six chromosomes), suggesting approximately 15% of sites may be attached in each mitotic cell.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C119, and C120 compare the number of cenH3 sites to microtubule attachments. While C70 and C119 are supported by the data (707 peaks identified) and established knowledge (C20), the calculation that ~15% of sites are attached (C120) is speculative without direct evidence. The authors acknowledge analyzing a diverse cell population, but no cell-type-specific or cell-cycle-specific analysis is provided to test this hypothesis. This requires additional experiments.

results.result: CenH3 nucleosomes in domains protect 135-155 bp of DNA, similar to canonical nucleosomes, suggesting cenH3 can incorporate into canonical-type nucleosomes away from centromeres and that domains may be distributed independently of the centromere.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C83, and C84 are supported by fragment size analysis of cenH3 nucleosomes in domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B) showing protection similar to canonical nucleosomes. The interpretation that these represent cenH3 incorporation into canonical nucleosomes (C83) is consistent with findings in other organisms (citations provided). The inference that domains are independent of centromeres (C84) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: The overall occupancy and positioning of most canonical nucleosomes and other DNA binding factors remained unchanged in knl-2(RNAi) embryos, with input chromatin showing the same correlation with wildtype as between wildtype replicates (R=0.971 and 0.969 vs R=0.973).
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by correlation analysis of input chromatin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) showing high correlation between wildtype and knl-2(RNAi) samples. This is an important control demonstrating that the reduced cenH3 signal in knl-2(RNAi) is specific to cenH3 sites and not due to general chromatin changes. The statistical analysis with large sample size (N=7,633,808 bins) is appropriate.

results.result: Multiple speculative mechanisms are proposed for centromere site selection and maintenance, including redundancy for faithful segregation, developmental regulation, H3.3-mediated inheritance, cenH3 'reservoirs', gap-filling by cenH3 nucleosomes, and transcription factor binding preventing nucleosome encroachment.
results.evaluation: Claims C121, C122, C126, C127, C132, C138, C139, C140, and C146 are explicitly speculative (using 'might', 'may', 'possibility') and represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. While these are reasonable interpretations of the data, they lack direct experimental support. For example, the gap-filling model (C132) and transcription factor role in maintenance (C146) are plausible but untested. These require follow-up experiments to validate.

results.result: CenH3 peaks are enriched in gene-poor regions, and only 174 insoluble chromatin peaks and 26 CENP-C peaks fall within previously defined domains, fewer than expected by chance (p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C66 are supported by genomic distribution analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) and peak overlap analysis. The statistical test showing fewer peaks in domains than expected by chance (p<0.001, C66) is appropriate. This finding reinforces the distinction between the discrete cenH3 peaks and the broad domains, supporting the polycentric model over the diffuse model.
